directive.name: planning
directive.description: Shift-left mindset: design for compliance before implementation

context.principle: Plans should be designed so code review passes on first attempt
Tests and documentation are part of the plan, not afterthoughts
Define implementation order: computers first, then capabilities, then orchestrator
Plan orchestrator structure upfront: identify domains and decide if multiple orchestrators are needed
Entry points should be thin composition roots - plan domain orchestrators for distinct concerns

process.rule: Verify planned architecture complies with code-standards before designing solution
Include test strategy with what to test and how to mock
List all modules with their architectural layer and verify dependency direction
Identify distinct domains and plan orchestrator structure (single vs multiple orchestrators)
For new applications: plan composition root structure and domain orchestrators upfront
When adding features to existing code: check if new domain warrants a new orchestrator

check.item: Plan verified against code-standards before implementation
All new modules assigned to correct architectural layer
Orchestrator structure planned (single vs domain orchestrators)
Distinct domains identified and assigned to orchestrators
Composition root identified and kept thin

example.code: ## Implementation Order 1. task-parser.computer.ts (no dependencies) 2. task-actions.computer.ts (no dependencies) 3. file-system.capability.ts (uses fs) 4. terminal.capability.ts (uses vscode) 5. tasks-view.capability.ts (injects computers) 6. extension.ts (orchestrates all) 7. Tests for computers

## Orchestrator Structure
### Domains Identified - **Tasks domain**: task CRUD, actions, status transitions - **Quicks domain**: quick task CRUD, simplified workflow - **Docs domain**: product/engineering docs browsing - **Terminal domain**: runtime selection, command execution
### Orchestrator Plan ``` src/ ├── extension.ts # Composition root (thin) ├── orchestrators/ │ ├── tasks.orchestrator.ts # ~200 lines │ ├── quicks.orchestrator.ts # ~100 lines │ ├── docs.orchestrator.ts # ~80 lines │ └── terminal.orchestrator.ts # ~60 lines ```
### Rationale - Domains have independent state and refresh cycles - Each domain has distinct capabilities/computers - Extension.ts stays under 100 lines (just wiring)
example.explanation: Plan orchestrator structure upfront for distinct domains

example.explanation: Missing orchestrator structure planning - extension.ts will become monolithic

example.code:
## New Feature: Add Settings Domain
### Analysis - New domain: user settings and preferences - Independent from existing domains - Has own state and persistence
### Plan 1. Create settings.computer.ts (pure settings logic) 2. Create settings.capability.ts (settings file I/O) 3. Create settings.orchestrator.ts (settings policy) 4. Wire into extension.ts composition root
### Composition Root Update ```typescript // extension.ts - add one line const settingsOrch = createSettingsOrchestrator(deps); ```
example.explanation: Plan new domain as separate orchestrator from the start
